INTRO_KICKER: For festival producers, venues, councils, and event agencies
INTRO_COL1: Oddtoe is an experiential design and generative-AI animation studio based in Melbourne, creating projection, installation, and animated work for events, venues, and galleries. This is a use case: how a festival producer or an events agency uses Oddtoe for a festival activation, from the first drawing to the day the gates open, and on to the day it comes down. The worked example is a walk-in inflatable entrance for a city festival, up for the run and packed away for next year. The same steps apply to a photo spot, a projection after dark, a parade piece, a seasonal takeover, or a festival mascot.
INTRO_COL2: Every festival looks like every festival. The same hired stage, the same lighting rig, and a client asking what will be different this year. Come to Oddtoe for the one thing on site that answers that question: an object drawn for your site, at a scale people walk through or stand under, built once and brought back every year. I am an installation artist and an inflatable designer, so the piece gets designed for where it stands, and a specialist maker builds it from my drawings. Bring the date and the site plan, and I will draw you the thing people queue up to photograph.
DRAWINGS_KICKER: Let's look at three steps in the process...
DRAWINGS_INTRO: Oddtoe handles the first three stages of an activation — where the idea starts, how it gets drawn (sketches, 3D panel patterns), and how the object sits on your site with a crowd moving through it.
DRAW1_BODY: I do love this stage. What is the one thing on site that people remember? What does the entrance say about the festival before anyone has seen a band? The idea, the feeling the object gives a crowd, and what your client needs it to say all get worked out here.
DRAW2_BODY: An inflatable is a pattern of panels before it is anything else. The form gets modelled in 3D, the seams get worked out, and the maker builds from those drawings. Here it is a walk-in dome, cut into the panels a sewing floor can follow. The shape you approve is the shape that arrives.
DRAW3_BODY: Working out where the object stands and how people move through it. The width of the doorway when a crowd arrives at once, what is behind it in every photo, where the blower and the power go so nobody trips on them. Oddtoe works out the site plan with you. Leave it until the morning of the load-in and you are solving it with a forklift waiting.

PANEL_TITLE: What an Activation Does to Your Numbers
PANEL_INTRO: An entrance at walk-in scale, the first thing people see from the queue. Nobody has to be told to take a picture of it. Out come the phones. So what does an activation like this do for your numbers? The things a producer already counts: gate numbers against last year, how many photos got tagged, how long people stayed on site, and the figures your client reads in the Monday debrief.

CIRCLES_TITLE: 6 IDEAS FOR YOUR NEXT FESTIVAL OR PRECINCT
CIRCLES_SUB: Six jobs a festival or a precinct has every year, and one object for each. Roll over a circle and pick the one your site could use.
CIRCLES_FOOT: Want one of these for your site? Send the date and the site plan. More on the characters in mascot design.
CIRCLE1_TITLE: The Entrance That Says It Has Started
CIRCLE1_BODY: A walk-in inflatable or a built gateway at the top of the queue. People know the festival has begun before they have seen a stage, and the first photo of the day is everyone walking through the mouth of it.
CIRCLE2_BODY: One object in the middle of the site that people queue to stand in front of. Big enough to see from the far stage, drawn so the best picture has a person in it, and placed so the photo says where it was taken.
CIRCLE3_BODY: Projection on the building or inside the hall for the evening session. The same characters from the entrance climb the facade after nine, so the site changes when the sun goes down and the night session looks like a different festival.
CIRCLE4_BODY: Carried, pulled or worn down the street. Oversized heads on poles, a puppet with a crew, or a character on a trolley. Built light enough for volunteers and packed into a crate for the next parade, and the one after that.
CIRCLE5_BODY: A Christmas or summer installation for a precinct or a group of venues, up for the season. The same object on the rooftop bar, in the laneway and on the socials for weeks, then packed for the same season next year.
CIRCLE6_BODY: A character that comes back every year. On the poster, the site map and the wristband, and walking the site in costume on the day. I draw the character and a specialist costume maker builds it from the drawings, so the poster and the costume are the same creature.
WHO_KICKER: Festival producers, councils, venues, and event agencies
WHO_COL1: Festival producers, city councils and precinct managers, event agencies, venue and hospitality groups, and the producers of conferences and galas. What they all have is a date and a space that needs one thing people remember. Festival producers need the entrance, the photo spot and the parade piece, and want them back next year without a new budget line. Councils and precinct managers run the Christmas takeover, the summer program and the laneway festival, and answer to the traders on the street.
WHO_COL2: Venues and hospitality groups bring venue openings, rooftop bars and seasonal takeovers. Those are events with a venue, so the same steps apply: one object, drawn for the room, up for the season. Conference and gala producers need the thing in the foyer that the delegates photograph, and the object on the night that the sponsor stands next to. Agencies working for any of the above are welcome too, and usually arrive with the client’s brief already written: see experiential marketing.
TIMELINE_TITLE: AN ENTRANCE, FROM BRIEF TO NEXT YEAR
STEP1_TITLE: Every festival looks like every festival
STEP1_BODY: A hired stage, a lighting rig, a row of food trucks, and a client who has seen all of it before and asks what will be different. The crowd has seen it before too. Nobody takes a photo of the lighting rig. So before anything gets drawn we settle one question: what is the one thing on this site that people will remember, and where does it stand?
STEP1_CRAFT: One question, settled before anything is drawn
STEP1_CAPTION: The brief, before anyone has measured a thing
STEP2_TITLE: The object, drawn into the site plan
STEP2_BODY: In this example it is a walk-in inflatable entrance. It gets drawn at scale on your site plan first, so you can see the width of the doorway against the queue and what is behind it in every photo. Then the form is modelled in 3D and cut into a pattern of panels, which is what the maker builds from. You approve a picture of the thing on your site before anything gets sewn.
STEP3_TITLE: Designed in Melbourne, built by the right maker
STEP3_BODY: Design happens in Melbourne. An inflatable is built by a specialist inflatable maker working from the panel drawings, with the blower, the anchor points and the repair kit that come with it. A built piece, a gateway or a carried object, comes out of my own workshop or a fabricator near you. Either way it is made to go up, come down, and go up again without anyone who was there for the first build.
STEP4_TITLE: Power, anchoring, and the site crew
STEP4_BODY: It arrives on the load-in day with the stages and the fencing. The site crew unpacks it, the anchor points go in, the blower gets power, and it stands up in the time it takes to fill. The install plan covers anchoring and wind, where the power runs, and what the site manager needs to see before the gates open. One number to ring if the crew has a question.
STEP4_CRAFT: Built to be installed by your crew
STEP5_BODY: For the run of the festival it is the first thing people see from the queue and the last thing they photograph on the way out. After dark the same characters can climb the venue in projection, operated live, so the site changes when the sun goes down. The festival gets its own photos and video of it, and so does everyone with a phone.
STEP5_CAPTION: A built sculpture lit by projection after dark
STEP6_TITLE: Packed down, stored, back next year
STEP6_BODY: A hired stage goes back on the truck on Monday, and next year you hire it again. A built object deflates, packs into its case, and comes out again for the same weekend next year, the winter edition, and the sister festival in the next town. The second year is the storage, the install crew and any repairs, which is a much easier line for a client to sign.

STEP6_CAPTION: The case it lives in between seasons
WHY_KICKER: The bit that is not a service
WHY_COL1: Street art is punk rock for visual artists. It gets seen by people who never decided to look at art that day, and a festival crowd is the same audience with a wristband on. They came for the music, and the object gets them anyway. Oddtoe has been inside a festival week too. I designed and built a carved sculpture with live projection for a kids’ comedy show at the Melbourne Comedy Festival, so I know what the days before opening look like from inside the venue.
WHY_COL2: I make my own work as well as client work, and big objects in public places are where I want to take that next. A walk-in entrance at a city festival is about the closest thing to what I would be making anyway, with a crowd already booked to see it. The practical upside for a producer is that the person designing the object has a stake in whether it works. I want the photo from the queue to be good for the same reason you do.

WYG_TITLE: What Does a Festival Actually Get?
WYG_COL1: The object, the drawings it came from, the install plan, and the photos and video from the run. All of it is yours to keep, case included, and it goes up again next year. • The object — in this example a walk-in inflatable entrance, with its blower, anchors and repair kit • The artwork — the same design flat, for the poster, the site map and social • An install plan your site crew works from, and the case it packs into • Photos and video from the run, for the client, the sponsors and next year’s pitch
WYG_COL2: People tend to forget about the artwork. Because the object is built from a finished character design, the festival also owns a drawing that works on the poster, the site map, a wristband and a phone screen without redrawing anything. It can be whatever the site needs: a walk-in inflatable, a built gateway, a festival mascot, a carried parade piece, or a projection on the venue after dark, with the same characters animated. They are designed together, so what climbs the wall at night is the same creature people walked through at the gate.
PKG1_BODY: We work out what the one thing on site is before we work out what to build. Bring the date, the site plan and the brief your client gave you.
PKG2_BODY: Character art, scale drawings, and the object standing on your site plan at the size it will be. You sign off on a picture your client can see.
PKG3_BODY: Anchoring and wind, power for the blower, and how a crowd moves through it. What the site manager needs to see before it goes up. Customs and freight, if it travels.
PKG4_BODY: Designed in Melbourne, built by a specialist inflatable maker from the drawings, or in my own workshop for a built piece. Made to pack down after the run and go up again next year without a technician.
PKG5_BODY: I run the job myself: visual progress reports, an install plan against your load-in day, and one number to ring when the site crew has a question.
CRED_TITLE: Why an Installation Artist Designs This
CRED_COL1: An installation artist makes work for a place. The object is finished when it stands where it was drawn to stand, with the crowd moving through it and the venue behind it in every photo. A hire catalogue cannot give you that, because nothing in it was drawn with your site in mind. Oddtoe designs at that scale: inflatables as a pattern of panels for a specialist maker to build, built pieces from my own workshop, and projection designed alongside the object so the two read as one thing after dark.
CRED_COL2: The precedent on this site is a 2.1-metre carved baobab with live projection, designed and built by Oddtoe for Babbling with Baobabs, a kids’ comedy show at the Melbourne Comedy Festival 2019, at Signal, the City of Melbourne venue. One object, made for one room, with the projection operated live for the run of the show. A festival entrance is the same job at a larger scale. The object is drawn for where it stands, built to be installed by the people already on site, and lit so it is a different thing after dark.

FAQ.q: What does this festival activation use case cover?
FAQ.a: A worked example of a festival activation. It follows one brief - a city festival with a date and a site that needs one thing people remember - from the first question through design, fabrication, install day, the run of the festival, and the pack-down for next year. It uses a walk-in inflatable entrance as the example, and a photo spot, a projection on the venue, a parade piece, a seasonal takeover or a festival mascot would follow the same shape.

FAQ.q: How long does a festival activation take?
FAQ.a: Six to eight weeks from brief to install day for a carried or built piece from the workshop. An inflatable or a mascot costume takes longer, because a specialist maker builds it from the drawings, so it needs to start earlier in your planning year. A rush is possible but it comes out of the design stage, which is the part worth protecting.

FAQ.q: What does a festival activation cost?
FAQ.a: Oddtoe does not publish prices. Cost is driven by what the object is, how large, whether the public walks through it, and where it has to travel. It is costed the same way as any other prop fabrication job. Send the date, the site plan and the brief and you get a quote.

FAQ.q: What does the site need on install day?
FAQ.a: Power for the blower, a spot for the anchor points, and a site crew for the load-in. The install plan covers anchoring and wind, where the power runs, and what the site manager needs to see before the gates open. I work through it with your site manager well before the week of the festival, so nothing gets settled with a forklift waiting.

FAQ.q: Can it travel to another city or country?
FAQ.a: Usually, yes. An inflatable packs small, and a built piece is designed to crate. Freight and customs get worked through with a freight agent as part of the job, including any treatment or certification the materials need. Often the simpler answer is to have it built near you, working from the drawings.

FAQ.q: Can we use it again next year?
FAQ.a: That is the point. It packs down into its case, goes into storage, and comes out for the same weekend next year, the winter edition, or the sister festival in the next town. The second year is the storage, the install crew and any repairs. Used a few times, one build can cost less than hiring something new for each one.

FAQ.q: Can you do the projection and animation as well?
FAQ.a: Yes, and they are designed together when the brief calls for it - the same characters from the entrance animated and projected on the venue after dark. See projection art and generative AI animation.
Oddtoe is based in Melbourne, Australia. Supplier and business contacts run through Berlin and Los Angeles, and those are the starting points for work in Europe and the United States.
